explain.h2: Every decision shows its work, including the rules that lost.
explain.subject: Akira (1988) · every rule that looked at it
explain.foot.3: matched on genre, failed on certification
explain.img-attr: The explanation panel for Akira: proposed category anime at 70% confidence, its TMDb metadata, and each rule with its conditions marked matched or not matched.
explain.p: A classification you cannot audit is one you cannot trust. Routarr records, condition by condition, what was expected and what was observed, for the winning rule and for every rule that did not win.
explain.p.2:
The engine itself never writes prose: it emits keys and parameters, and the text is rendered
        in your language at display time. The justifications are translated in all 26 languages,
        not frozen in English at the moment they were computed.
faq.lead: Most of the answers below are no, which is the most useful thing this section has to say.
faq.m.2: The root folder, not the name
faq.m.3: The Arrs are a source of their own
faq.m.4: Two fields, through their own API
faq.m.5: No outbound request nobody asked for
faq.p: Global dry-run is on from the first launch, the option to move files on disk is unchecked by default, and applying past a threshold needs an explicit confirmation. Without the disk-move option, Routarr only re-points the library entry and leaves the files where they are.
faq.p.2: A move changes the root folder above your title and keeps the folder name exactly as it is, so a library pointed at it by Plex or Jellyfin keeps working.
faq.p.3: Radarr and Sonarr are a metadata source of their own. They already report genres, original language and certification, and Routarr reads them from the same response it syncs the library with. For keywords and origin country, AniList needs no key either. TMDb, OMDb and TheTVDB are there if you want them. Sources are an ordered list, so you decide which one wins when they disagree.
faq.p.4: It deliberately does not try. Routarr never manages downloads, indexers or the library itself. It writes exactly two things through the Arr API, the root folder and the path, then asks for a rescan.
faq.p.5:
No telemetry, no analytics, no update check. The only outbound calls go to your Radarr and Sonarr
          instances, to the metadata sources you enable (TMDb, AniList, Jikan, OMDb, TheTVDB), to your OpenID
          Connect provider if you use one, and to a notification webhook if you set one.
faq.p.6: Including under a sub-path. Set ROUTARR_BASE_PATH=/routarr and the API, the interface and the webhook URLs all move with it, with no image rebuild.
faq.p.7:
One Docker image for amd64 and arm64, so a Pi or an N100 is enough. Storage is a single
          SQLite file. There is no database service to run.

features.img-attr: The dashboard: 14 movies, 6 series, 4 active rules, 13 pending decisions, full TMDb metadata coverage, and both Radarr and Sonarr instances reporting as connected.
features.p: One dashboard over every connected instance: what is tracked, what is enriched, what is waiting for you.
features.p.2: Any number of Radarr and Sonarr servers, each with its own sync interval, folders and mappings.
features.p.3: A per-instance secret URL. New additions are synced, enriched and evaluated immediately instead of at the next poll.
features.p.4: Pin a title to a category and the engine stops arguing. An override outranks every rule, and any applied move can be undone from the history.
features.p.5: Library size, decisions per category and status, instance health, and the state of the guardrails, all behind the same API key.
features.p.6: One generic JSON webhook for Discord, Gotify, ntfy or Apprise, fired on a state change and never on a loop.
features.p.7: Rules, categories, mappings and overrides export as JSON and travel between installations. Arr API keys are AES-256-GCM-encrypted and never leave.
folders.figcaption: Seven folders across two instances, each mapped to a category.
folders.img-attr: The root folders screen: seven folders across Radarr and Sonarr, each showing its path, free space, accessible state and the category it is mapped to.
folders.p: Routarr never creates a library layout. It reads the root folders Radarr and Sonarr declare, and where you want a destination they do not list you type it here and it is marked as such. Either way you attach it to a category you named, and a declared folder takes its free space and reachability from the synced folder it sits under.
folders.foot.2: three declared here, four read from the Arrs
folders.p.2:
Free space and reachability come straight from the Arr. Two folders claiming the same
        category on one instance is refused rather than silently resolved, and a category no folder
        provides is reported before it can quietly skip your media.

how.h2: Four steps, and you can stop after the third.
how.foot: one step writes to your library
how.foot.2: and the global dry-run switch blocks that one at the server
how.p: Nothing is written until an explicit action asks for it, and the global dry-run switch blocks writes at the server no matter what the interface does.
how.p.2: Reads films, series, tags and root folders from every Radarr and Sonarr you connect. An empty response is never treated as a mass deletion.
how.p.3: Genres, language and certification come free with the sync. Add TMDb for keywords and country: one call per title, cached, deduplicated, bounded concurrency.
how.p.4: Rules run by ascending priority, and the first match wins. Exclusions veto a rule that otherwise matched. Anything unmatched falls to your default category.
how.p.5: Moves are grouped per instance and target folder, written through the Arr API, then rescanned. Every applied move can be reverted.
page.figcaption: A dry-run: 13 proposed moves, each with its why, and nothing written yet.
page.h1: Every title in the right folder, decided by your rules.
page.img-attr: The dry-run simulation screen: 20 items evaluated, 13 moves required, 7 already correct, and a table of proposed moves with source folder, target folder, matching rule, confidence and justification.
page.p: Routarr reads your libraries, enriches every title from the metadata sources you order, and decides which root folder it belongs in. You see the whole plan first, and it writes only when you say so.
page.p.2: Self-hosted. One container. Dry-run is on until you turn it off.
page.p.3: First matching rule wins. Exclusions can veto. Everything is explained.
page.p.maturity: In active development. The rule engine and the safety rails are stable, and the interface will keep moving.
rules.p: Combine conditions with ALL or ANY, add explicit exclusions, order rules by priority. Genre, keyword, original language, country, certification, year, status, current folder, title, external ids and age, plus the signals only your Arr has: tags, Sonarr's series type, size on disk and season count.
rules.p.2:
Rules export and import as JSON, so they can be versioned outside the application, and a
        preview shows exactly what a change would do before it is saved.
rules.p.3: Exclusions are why this works. "Japanese animation" would swallow My Neighbor Totoro. The deliberate exclusion of G-rated certifications hands it to kids instead, and the interface says so.
safety.h2: Nothing is written until six gates agree.
safety.p: Routarr moves files on disk. Every one of these is on by default, they run in this order, and the first one to object stops the rest. The first alone is enough to make the whole application read-only.
safety.reach.p: A destination that did not answer the last time anyone looked. A NAS that has spun down cannot be told from a dead disk, so this one asks rather than refuses.
safety.capacity.p: The plan weighed against the free space the sync already recorded, counting only the bytes that cross a filesystem.
safety.legend.2: raises a question under its own name, which you answer
safety.p.2: On from the first launch. While it is on, nothing is written, whatever you click and whatever automation is enabled.
safety.p.3: A hard ceiling on how many items one apply can touch. Reclassifying a whole library is a separate, deliberate action.
safety.p.4: Past a number you choose, a second explicit confirmation is required, recognised by a stable error code rather than by matching English text.
safety.p.5: Each decision is checked again against the current rules and library. A proposal the rules no longer justify is refused, not executed.
safety.p.6: Automatic application exists, and it is off by default. When enabled it touches only titles with no files on disk yet, the case where changing the folder is a metadata write and nothing moves. Anything already downloaded stays in the human queue.
start.p:
One image carries the backend and the interface, for amd64 and arm64: a Synology or
        QNAP NAS, Unraid, TrueNAS, a Raspberry Pi or a plain VPS. Save the compose file, start it,
        and the first run needs no configuration file.
start.step: The container runs as uid 1000 and drops every capability, so the volume has to belong to it.
start.step.2: One image, backend and interface together. Nothing else to install.
start.step.3: The key is generated on first start and written beside the database. The log prints it once, the file keeps it.
start.step.4: Global dry-run is already on. Nothing can be written until you turn it off.
start.p.2:
Then: connect your Arrs, map your folders to categories, write a rule and preview it,
            run a dry-run, and turn the global dry-run off only when you agree with the plan.
start.p.3: Back up routarr.db and routarr.key together. Without the key, the stored Arr credentials cannot be recovered.
why.h2: Your Arrs already know all of this. None of it picks a folder.
why.p.2: Routarr is that missing decision layer: one place where the logic lives, using the folders your Arrs already have. On a webhook it decides before the download even lands, while the folder is still empty and nothing has to move.
